modules.title: Module 1: Foreign Policy and Nigeria's Position in World Affairs
modules.html:
Foreign policy is the totality of the principles, decisions and actions by which a state pursues and protects its interests in its relations with other states and international organisations.

Objectives of Nigeria's Foreign Policy (Section 19, 1999 Constitution)

  1. Promotion and protection of the national interest
  2. Promotion of African integration and support for African unity
  3. Promotion of international cooperation for the consolidation of universal peace and mutual respect among nations
  4. Respect for international law and treaty obligations, and the seeking of settlement of disputes by negotiation, mediation, conciliation, arbitration and adjudication
  5. Promotion of a just world economic order

Determinants of Foreign Policy

Internal (Domestic)External
Size, population and geographical locationThe international system and balance of power
Economic and military capabilityMembership of international organisations
Nature of government and leadership styleActions and policies of other states
Public opinion, the press and pressure groupsInternational law and treaty obligations
Historical and cultural tiesGlobal economic conditions
Ideology and national interestActivities of multinational corporations

Principles of Nigerian Foreign Policy

  • Africa as the centrepiece of foreign policy
  • Non-alignment — refusal to belong to either the Western or Eastern bloc during the Cold War
  • Respect for the sovereign equality of states and non-interference in internal affairs
  • Total decolonisation of Africa and opposition to apartheid, racism and colonialism
  • Peaceful settlement of disputes and support for functional cooperation
  • Good neighbourliness and economic diplomacy (notably from 1985)

Achievements

Leadership in the creation of ECOWAS (1975); the Technical Aid Corps; the ECOMOG peacekeeping missions in Liberia (1990) and Sierra Leone; sustained financial and moral support for liberation movements in Angola, Mozambique, Zimbabwe, Namibia and South Africa; nationalisation of Barclays Bank and British Petroleum interests over Britain's Rhodesia and apartheid policies; contributions to UN peacekeeping from the Congo (1960) onwards; and peaceful compliance with the ICJ judgment on the Bakassi Peninsula.

Non-Alignment

Non-alignment means refusing to be tied to any power bloc while retaining freedom to judge each issue on its merits. Founded at Belgrade in 1961 by Nehru, Nasser, Tito, Nkrumah and Sukarno, its aims were to avoid entanglement in the Cold War, promote decolonisation and world peace, and secure economic cooperation. Nigeria's non-alignment is often described as "dynamic" rather than passive.

examples.q: Why is Africa described as the centrepiece of Nigeria's foreign policy?
examples.a: Because Nigeria's most consistent commitment since 1960 has been to African liberation, unity and stability. Nigeria funded liberation movements in Southern Africa, campaigned relentlessly against apartheid, expelled and nationalised the assets of firms tied to racist regimes, initiated and largely finances ECOWAS, and bore the cost of ECOMOG peacekeeping in Liberia and Sierra Leone. Critics argue this altruism was expensive and yielded limited domestic benefit, a criticism often summarised as 'big brother diplomacy'.

examples.q: How did Nigeria demonstrate respect for international law in the Bakassi dispute?
examples.a: Nigeria and Cameroon submitted the sovereignty dispute over the Bakassi Peninsula to the International Court of Justice. When the Court ruled in Cameroon's favour in 2002, Nigeria, despite domestic opposition, complied through the Greentree Agreement of 2006 and completed the handover in 2008. This peaceful settlement of a potentially explosive dispute reinforced Nigeria's standing as a law-abiding member of the international community.

modules.title: Module 2: The United Nations Organisation
modules.html:
The United Nations was established on 24 October 1945 in San Francisco, replacing the defunct League of Nations. Nigeria joined on 7 October 1960 as the 99th member.

Aims and Objectives

  1. To maintain international peace and security
  2. To develop friendly relations among nations based on sovereign equality and self-determination
  3. To achieve international cooperation in solving economic, social, cultural and humanitarian problems
  4. To promote respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms
  5. To serve as a centre for harmonising the actions of nations

Principal Organs

OrganCompositionMain Function
General AssemblyAll member states, one vote eachDebates any matter, approves the budget, admits members
Security Council15 members: 5 permanent (USA, UK, France, Russia, China) with veto power, 10 elected for two yearsPrimary responsibility for international peace and security; authorises sanctions and peacekeeping
Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC)54 membersCoordinates economic, social and humanitarian work and the specialised agencies
Trusteeship CouncilSuspended in 1994Supervised trust territories until they attained independence
International Court of Justice15 judges at The HagueSettles legal disputes between states; gives advisory opinions
SecretariatHeaded by the Secretary-GeneralAdministration and day-to-day operations

Specialised Agencies

WHO, UNESCO, UNICEF, FAO, ILO, IMF, World Bank (IBRD), IAEA, UNHCR, UNDP and UNIDO.

Achievements and Problems

Achievements: prevention of a third world war, decolonisation of over 80 territories, peacekeeping in the Congo, Cyprus, Lebanon, Liberia and elsewhere, humanitarian relief, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948), and campaigns against disease and illiteracy. Problems: the veto power paralysing the Security Council, inadequate funding and unpaid dues, absence of a standing army, domination by the great powers, disregard of resolutions by powerful states, and the slow pace of Security Council reform.

examples.q: Explain how the veto power weakens the United Nations.
examples.a: Any one of the five permanent members of the Security Council can block a substantive resolution regardless of the support of the other fourteen members. This means that where a great power or its ally is involved in a conflict, effective UN action becomes impossible, as seen in various Cold War and contemporary crises. The result is selective enforcement, loss of credibility, and pressure for reform of the Council's composition and voting rules.

examples.q: State two ways Nigeria has contributed to the United Nations.
examples.a: First, Nigeria has been a major troop contributor to UN peacekeeping operations since the Congo mission of 1960, serving in Lebanon, the former Yugoslavia, Somalia, Darfur and elsewhere. Second, Nigeria has served repeatedly as a non-permanent member of the Security Council and has been a consistent voice for decolonisation, anti-apartheid measures and the reform of the Council to include permanent African representation.

modules.title: Module 3: The African Union, ECOWAS and the Commonwealth
modules.html:
From OAU to African Union

The Organisation of African Unity was founded on 25 May 1963 in Addis Ababa by 32 states, reconciling the radical Casablanca bloc and the moderate Monrovia bloc. It was replaced by the African Union, launched at Durban in 2002 following the Sirte Declaration of 1999.

Objectives of the AU: to achieve greater unity and solidarity among African states; defend sovereignty, territorial integrity and independence; accelerate political and socio-economic integration; promote peace, security and stability; promote democratic principles, good governance, human rights and sustainable development; and promote cooperation in all fields of human activity.

Organs: the Assembly of Heads of State and Government, the Executive Council of Ministers, the Pan-African Parliament, the Commission (secretariat) in Addis Ababa, the Peace and Security Council, the African Court of Justice and Human Rights, the Permanent Representatives Committee, ECOSOCC and the specialised technical committees. NEPAD and the African Peer Review Mechanism are its development instruments.

Achievements: completion of decolonisation and the dismantling of apartheid, mediation in border and civil conflicts, peacekeeping in Somalia, Sudan and Burundi, suspension of governments that come to power through coups, and the launch of the African Continental Free Trade Area. Problems: inadequate funding and dependence on donors, member-state sovereignty limiting enforcement, ideological differences, coups and instability, poor infrastructure and communication, and the influence of former colonial powers.

ECOWAS

The Economic Community of West African States was formed by the Treaty of Lagos on 28 May 1975, largely through the initiative of Nigeria's General Gowon and Togo's President Eyadema. It has 15 member states with headquarters in Abuja.

Aims: promotion of trade and economic cooperation; free movement of persons, goods, services and capital; establishment of a common external tariff and eventual customs union and monetary union; harmonisation of agricultural, industrial, transport and energy policies; and improvement of the standard of living of West Africans.

Achievements: abolition of visa requirements for citizens of member states for stays up to 90 days and the introduction of the ECOWAS passport and travel certificate; the ECOWAS Trade Liberalisation Scheme; ECOMOG peacekeeping in Liberia, Sierra Leone, Guinea-Bissau and The Gambia; the ECOWAS Court of Justice and Parliament; and progress towards the single currency (the ECO) through WAMZ.

Problems: the language and colonial divide between anglophone and francophone states with the competing UEMOA and the CFA franc, smuggling and border closures, differing levels of development, poor transport links, political instability and military coups, insecurity, and over-dependence on Nigeria for funding.

The Commonwealth of Nations

A voluntary association of some 56 independent states, most formerly under British rule, headed symbolically by the British monarch. Aims: promotion of democracy, good governance, human rights, the rule of law and development through consultation and cooperation. Instruments include the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM), the Commonwealth Secretariat in London, the Commonwealth Games and technical assistance schemes. Nigeria was suspended in 1995 after the execution of Ken Saro-Wiwa and readmitted in 1999. Weaknesses: it lacks enforcement machinery, its resolutions are non-binding, and members pursue divergent interests.

examples.q: Assess Nigeria's role in the formation and funding of ECOWAS.
examples.a: Nigeria, under General Gowon, worked with President Eyadema of Togo to draft and promote the treaty signed in Lagos on 28 May 1975, using its oil wealth and diplomatic weight to persuade francophone neighbours tied to France. Since then Nigeria has hosted the secretariat in Abuja, contributed the largest share of the budget, and supplied the bulk of ECOMOG troops and funding in Liberia, Sierra Leone and The Gambia. The dependence on Nigeria is also a weakness, since instability or economic downturn in Nigeria stalls the community's programmes.

examples.q: Why has the free movement protocol of ECOWAS not been fully realised?
examples.a: Border officials continue to demand illegal payments and impose restrictions, national governments periodically close borders over smuggling and security concerns, and there is a lack of harmonised documentation and infrastructure. Deeper causes include the anglophone-francophone divide with the parallel UEMOA framework, unequal levels of development that generate fear of labour influx, and insecurity from insurgency and cross-border crime.

quiz.q: Foreign policy is best defined as
options: The principles and actions guiding a state's relations with other states
The budget of the foreign ministry
The treaties signed by the United Nations
quiz.solution: Foreign policy is the set of principles and actions by which a state pursues its interests abroad.

quiz.q: The centrepiece of Nigeria's foreign policy is
quiz.solution: Since 1960 Nigeria has made African unity, liberation and stability the focus of its diplomacy.

options: Refusal to join any power bloc
quiz.solution: Non-aligned states avoided commitment to either the Western or Eastern bloc during the Cold War.

quiz.q: The United Nations was established in
quiz.solution: The UN Charter came into force on 24 October 1945.

quiz.q: The organ of the UN with primary responsibility for international peace and security is the
quiz.solution: The Security Council can authorise sanctions and peacekeeping to maintain peace.

quiz.q: The veto power in the UN is exercised by
options: All members of the General Assembly
The five permanent members of the Security Council
quiz.solution: The USA, UK, France, Russia and China can each block a substantive Security Council resolution.

quiz.q: The International Court of Justice sits at
quiz.solution: The ICJ, with 15 judges, is located at The Hague in the Netherlands.

quiz.q: The OAU was founded in Addis Ababa in
quiz.solution: Thirty-two African states founded the OAU on 25 May 1963.

quiz.q: The African Union was formally launched in
quiz.solution: The AU was inaugurated at Durban in 2002 following the Sirte Declaration of 1999.

quiz.q: ECOWAS was established by the Treaty of Lagos in
quiz.solution: The Treaty of Lagos was signed on 28 May 1975.

quiz.q: The headquarters of the ECOWAS Commission is in
quiz.solution: The ECOWAS Commission is headquartered in Abuja, Nigeria.
ECOMOG's first major peacekeeping deployment was to Liberia in 1990.

quiz.q: Which of these is a determinant of foreign policy?
options: Number of political parties in a state
quiz.solution: Size, population, economic strength and military capability shape a state's international influence.

quiz.q: Nigeria was suspended from the Commonwealth in 1995 because of
options: The annulment of the June 12 election
The execution of Ken Saro-Wiwa and the Ogoni nine
quiz.solution: The Abacha regime's execution of Ken Saro-Wiwa led to Nigeria's suspension at the Auckland CHOGM.

quiz.q: Nigeria handed over the Bakassi Peninsula to Cameroon following a judgment of the
quiz.solution: The ICJ ruled in 2002 and Nigeria completed the handover in 2008 under the Greentree Agreement.

quiz.q: A major problem of the African Union is
options: Reluctance of members to surrender sovereignty
quiz.solution: Member states guard their sovereignty jealously, which limits the AU's power to enforce decisions.
